explain.say: Why can poverty pass from parents to children, and then to grandchildren? It is not because people do not try. Look at the board. It is a circle, and economists call it the poverty trap, or the cycle of poverty. Let us follow it round.

explain.say: See the first stop, low income? Income means the money a family earns. With low income, a family cannot afford enough good food or medicine. Now look at poor food and health: hungry or sick children find it hard to concentrate, and sick adults miss work. Can you see how one problem leads to the next?

explain.say: See less schooling? When money is tight, children may leave school early to work or care for younger siblings, or the family cannot pay for uniforms and books. Without school, they have fewer skills. Why might a family make that hard choice?

explain.say: Now look at low-paid work. With fewer skills, the grown-up children often find only low-paid jobs, which brings us back to low income, and the circle turns again for the next generation. Where in the circle do you think it could be broken?

faq.a: The poverty trap, or cycle of poverty, is when the effects of being poor, like poor health and less schooling, make it hard to earn more, so poverty continues and can pass to the next generation.
asks: What is the cycle of poverty?

faq.q: Why does low income lead to more problems?
faq.a: With little money, families may not afford enough nutritious food, health care, safe housing or school costs. These gaps then make it harder to work and learn.

faq.q: Why do poor children sometimes leave school?
faq.a: Families may need children to earn money or care for siblings, or cannot pay for uniforms, books, transport or fees. Free schooling and school meals help keep children in class.
asks: Why is school hard for poor children?

faq.q: Why do people with less schooling earn less?
faq.a: Many better-paid jobs need reading, maths or special skills. Without them, people are often limited to low-paid, insecure work.

faq.q: How can the poverty trap be broken?
faq.a: Ideas include free education and school meals, health care, cash transfers to families, small loans for businesses, and fair wages. Economists test and debate which work best in each place.

facts: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Economics for experiments testing ways to reduce global poverty.
Mexico's Progresa programme (1997), now copied in many countries, paid families cash on condition that children attended school and health check-ups.

options.show: Each problem leads to the next and back to the start

quiz.why: Low income leads to poor health and less schooling, which lead to low pay and low income again.

wrong.1: The circle shows causes linking, not movement.
wrong.2: The circle shows that it repeats, even across generations.

quiz.say: Which of these could help break the cycle at the "less schooling" stop?
quiz.show: What could help at the schooling stop?
quiz.why: Free meals give families a reason to send children to school and help them learn.

wrong.0: Higher fees would push more children out of school.
wrong.2: Longer walks make attending school harder.
